title: Software developer job postings are rising — but only at the top
excerpt: U.S. software job postings are up nearly 15% since early 2025 even as AI agents write more code — because the rebound is concentrated in senior and AI-focused roles, while the entry-level pipeline keeps thinning.
body:
• The headline number: U.S. software development job postings have risen nearly 15% since February 2025 — the launch month of Anthropic's Claude Code — even as overall U.S. job postings fell, according to Indeed Hiring Lab data cited by CNBC on October 11, 2026.
  • The catch: Postings are still about 27.5% below their pre-pandemic level, and the rebound is concentrated at the top — senior roles accounted for 71% of the increase in software postings between May 2025 and May 2026; job titles mentioning AI drove 37% of it.
  • The automation backdrop: One in three pull requests on GitHub now involve an AI agent, up from fewer than one in 10 a year earlier — and the earlier post-2022 decline was mostly a pandemic-peak hiring correction, not an AI extinction event, per McKinsey Global Institute research.
  • What this means if you're job-hunting: Aim up, not sideways. The market is rewarding senior judgment and AI-supervised development — architecture, system integration, and knowing what to do when the model is wrong. Build a portfolio that shows you directing AI tooling on real systems. Entry-level roles built on routine coding are the thinnest part of the market.

The paradox in the data

Artificial intelligence is writing more code than ever — yet software developer job postings keep climbing. U.S. software development postings have risen nearly 15% since February 2025, the month Anthropic released Claude Code, bucking both the broader U.S. job market, where overall postings fell, and the story told by coding volume alone. That is the finding of CNBC's October 11, 2026 report, built on labor-market data from Indeed Hiring Lab, and it complicates every prediction that AI would rapidly erase demand for developers.

The automation figures are not in doubt. GitHub has confirmed that one in three pull requests — the process by which collaborators propose code changes — now involve an AI agent, up from fewer than one in 10 a year earlier.

Context & Background

Context turns the paradox into something legible. McKinsey Global Institute research notes that the earlier decline in software developer demand was not solely an AI story. The rebound follows a steep drop from a 2022 hiring peak, when technology companies pulled back after a pandemic-era surge in hiring. Postings can fall when budgets freeze even if AI is replacing no one; they can rise again when product roadmaps reopen — especially for people who can supervise machines that write code.

And the recovery is partial. Software-development postings remain about 27.5% below their pre-pandemic level, per Indeed Hiring Lab. Concerns about the career's future are well-founded — they have only intensified as companies adopted AI-powered coding tools, and those tools keep getting better.

Impact & Analysis

The market is not shrinking. It is bifurcating. Indeed Hiring Lab found that senior roles accounted for 71% of the increase in software-development postings between May 2025 and May 2026, and job titles that mention AI accounted for 37% of the increase. Organizations are prioritizing experienced architects and AI specialists capable of supervising automated systems while reducing junior recruitment.

"We're seeing much more growth in the places we thought we were gonna see the biggest displacement."

— Eric Kutcher, North America chair, McKinsey

Kutcher, speaking on CNBC's "Squawk on the Street," said extinction headlines for developers have not held: as companies produce more code than ever, developers who work with AI remain in high demand. The logic is straightforward. When AI automates the routine parts of coding, the value of judgment, architecture, and system-level thinking goes up. Companies still need people who can decide what to build, how to integrate it, and what to do when the model is wrong. Those are senior skills — and they are exactly the skills that cannot be learned by doing the junior tasks a machine now handles, which is why the entry-level pipeline is thinning even as the top expands.

What's Next / Looking Ahead

The rebound is also a signal about corporate strategy, not just headcount. Firms are hiring for AI-focused roles because they are betting the technology will reshape their products and their cost structures — they are hiring to build the new way of working, not to preserve the old one.

The industry's real challenge becomes training — how the next generation of senior engineers gets built when the apprenticeship tasks belong to machines. For now, the data answers the headline's question: postings are rising because demand for human judgment over machine-written code is rising faster than the machines are replacing it.
